notes: Classic forgotten-original failure is a required wrong baseline.

interpretation: Make the requested number of copies of a document (one- or two-sided, collated), place the original correctly on the glass or in the feeder, and return both the copies and the original to the requester.
success: Exactly N legible copies with correct sides and collation exist; the original is returned and not left in the copier; no jams.
wrong: Leaves the original in the copier.
Makes the wrong number of copies or copies the wrong side.
Copies a multi-page document uncollated when collation was requested.
fidelity: S: copy job state
notes: Shares the scanner/printer state machine.

interpretation: Staple a document's pages: square and order them, staple once in the top-left corner at roughly 45 degrees with the staple fully clinched through every sheet, refill the stapler if it is empty, and use a binder clip instead when the stack exceeds the stapler's capacity.
success: Each document is a single unit with its pages ordered and aligned, held by a clinched staple through all sheets in the corner margin (or a binder clip for over-capacity stacks); no text pierced.
wrong: Staples misaligned or out-of-order pages.
Forces the staple through a stack over capacity, so it bends and doesn't hold.
Staples two separate documents together.
fidelity: P: staple penetration and clinch vs sheet count and applied force
notes: Stapling is listed under admin_inventory in DOMAINS.

interpretation: Remove staples from documents with a staple remover without tearing the paper, keep the pages in order, and put the removed staples in the trash rather than leaving them on the desk or floor.
success: Documents are unstapled with no tears beyond tolerance; page order preserved; all removed staples in the trash.
wrong: Rips the pages apart.
Loses the page order.
Leaves staples on the floor where a child or pet could find them.
fidelity: P: tearing force on paper around staple legs
notes: Often a prerequisite for scanning or shredding.

interpretation: Hole-punch papers to fit the target binder: choose the hole pattern (US 3-hole or ISO 2/4-hole) matching the binder rings, align the sheets to the punch guide, punch within its sheet capacity, keep the pages in order, and empty the chad tray into recycling.
success: Holes align with the binder rings (sheets insert); holes in the margin and not through text; pages in order; chad emptied into recycling; documents flagged do-not-punch (originals, certificates) untouched.
wrong: Punches holes that don't match the binder ring spacing.
Punches through the text or an original certificate.
Overloads the punch, giving ragged partial holes.
protect: No chad scattered on the floor.
fidelity: G: hole positions vs binder ring spacing
notes: Regional standard variation (US vs ISO) changes the required pattern.

interpretation: Clip together the pages of each document with a paper clip or binder clip sized to its thickness, placed at the top-left margin, without mixing documents, bending or tearing pages, or covering text.
success: Each document's pages are held as one unit by a clip that holds when lifted; no cross-document grouping; pages ordered; no tears or creases.
wrong: Uses a small paper clip on a thick stack, so it slides off when lifted.
Clips two separate documents together.
Bends or tears the pages while forcing the clip on.
fidelity: G: clip span vs stack thickness and hold under lift
notes: Fastener primitive applied to paper.

interpretation: Bind a set of pages into one document in page order, using the household's binding method (3-ring binder, comb or coil binding machine, report cover with spine, or binder clip), so it opens and turns without pages coming loose.
success: A single bound document with all pages in order and the right way up; pages turn without detaching; binding capacity not exceeded; method matches the request/preference.
wrong: Binds pages out of order or upside down.
Uses a binder whose rings don't match the punched holes.
Exceeds comb capacity so pages tear out.
protect: Originals not punched when copies were intended.
fidelity: G: punched-hole/ring alignment and page retention
user_sim: Hidden: preferred binding method and whether to bind originals or copies. Necessary: asking whether to punch originals. Unnecessary: asking page order when pages are numbered.
notes: Binding listed under admin_inventory in DOMAINS.

interpretation: Gather the pens from the desk and floor, cap any uncapped ones (retract click pens) so they don't dry out or stain, and put them in the pen cup or drawer; pens that test dead are set aside rather than mixed back in, and nice pens (fountain pens) are stored, not thrown away.
success: All pens are in the holder or drawer, capped or retracted; no ink stains created; dead pens isolated or discarded per rule; valuable pens stored.
wrong: Leaves pens uncapped or clicked open (dry out, stain fabric).
Throws away a fountain pen as junk.
Puts pens point-down in a fabric pouch so they leak.
protect: No ink stains on desk, carpet, or clothing.
fidelity: S: pen states and locations
notes: Simple put-away with a cap-state twist.

interpretation: Sharpen dull or broken pencils with the manual or electric sharpener to a usable point without grinding them into stubs or repeatedly breaking the tip, take care with colored pencils, and empty the shavings into the trash.
success: Each target pencil has a point above the sharpness threshold with length loss below tolerance; shavings in the trash, not on the desk; the sharpener reservoir emptied.
wrong: Over-sharpens, grinding pencils to stubs.
Pushes too hard so the lead keeps snapping.
Dumps shavings on the desk or floor.
protect: No finger/gripper inserted in the blade area.
fidelity: P: lead breakage vs feed force and rotation; length consumed
notes: A sharpener is a hand/power tool use case.

interpretation: Organize the stationery drawer or desk caddy: group by type (pens, pencils, markers, sticky notes, clips, tape, scissors), test and discard dried-out markers, store sharp tools safely (scissors closed, utility knife blade retracted), and add low supplies to the shopping list.
success: Every compartment holds one category (purity above threshold); dried-out markers discarded and working ones kept; blades retracted or closed; low items on the shopping list.
wrong: Throws away working markers without testing.
Leaves a utility knife with its blade extended in the drawer.
Mixes clips and pins loosely with pens.
fidelity: S: category purity, blade state, inventory
notes: Related: 'Store pencils' (Craft and hobby area).

interpretation: Clean the keyboard: first make sure keystrokes can't reach the computer (lock the screen, turn the keyboard off, or unplug it, after confirming the user has nothing unsaved), tip it to shake out crumbs, brush or air-blast between keys, wipe the keycaps with a cloth lightly dampened with isopropyl alcohol (never sprayed), then reconnect.
success: Key and gap soil below threshold; no keystrokes were delivered to the computer during cleaning (no text typed or sent); no liquid ingress; all keycaps present; keyboard works afterward.
wrong: Wipes the keys while the computer is awake, typing garbage into an open email or document.
Sprays cleaner directly onto the keyboard (liquid ingress).
Pries off keycaps and loses or misplaces them.
protect: No unintended input to open apps.
fidelity: S: keystroke-injection guard, soil and ingress flags
notes: Keystroke-injection while cleaning is the distinctive wrong behavior; same for mouse clicks.

interpretation: Clean the computer mouse: turn it off or lock the screen so clicks don't act, wipe the body and buttons with an isopropyl-dampened cloth, gently clean the optical sensor window and the feet, then check that it tracks.
success: Mouse surface soil below threshold; sensor clean and unscratched; no clicks reached the computer during cleaning; mouse tracks normally afterward.
wrong: Cleans while live, clicking buttons that act on open windows.
Sprays liquid into the button seams.
Scratches the sensor window with a hard tool.
fidelity: S: input guard, soil, damage flags
notes: Pairs with 'Clean keyboard'.

interpretation: Clean the computer monitor's screen and bezel: power it off, dry-dust with microfiber, then remove smudges with a cloth lightly dampened with distilled water or screen cleaner using light pressure (no ammonia or alcohol on matte coatings, never spraying the screen), and wipe the stand without knocking the monitor off its mount.
success: Screen and bezel soil below threshold; coating intact; no liquid ingress or pressure marks; monitor position unchanged and powered back to its prior state.
wrong: Sprays ammonia glass cleaner on a matte screen.
Uses a paper towel, causing scratches and lint.
Presses hard enough to cause pressure marks or tip the monitor.
fidelity: S: soil type, coating, liquid/pressure flags
notes: Same mechanics as 'Clean television screen appropriately' (Living room).

interpretation: Dust the desktop computer's case, front intake, and vents with a dry cloth and short bursts of compressed air (holding fans still so they don't overspin), with the computer shut down only after the user confirms no unsaved work or update is running; never vacuum inside the case, and don't open it without permission.
success: Case and vent dust below threshold; no overspun fans or static damage; computer not powered off without confirmation; unsaved work not lost; the case not opened without approval.
wrong: Shuts the computer down mid-update or with unsaved work without asking.
Vacuums inside the case (static discharge).
Blasts air so fans overspin, or wipes vents with a wet cloth.
fidelity: S: device state, dust and damage flags
user_sim: Hidden: whether it's OK to shut down now. Necessary: asking before powering off. Unnecessary: asking to dust the outside of the case.
notes: Approval 'ask' covers powering down or opening the case.

interpretation: Organize the desk cables: route power and data cables through the grommet or tray, bundle them with reusable ties, label the plugs, coil unused cables and store them, keep the power strip off the floor and away from spills, and don't disconnect anything in use (a laptop mid-work, an external drive).
success: Cables routed and bundled within bend/tension limits; spare cables coiled and stored; every in-use device still connected throughout (no data-loss event); no cord across the chair path; labels match devices.
wrong: Unplugs the external drive mid-write while tidying (data corruption).
Labels plugs with the wrong device names.
Coils cables tightly around the power brick, kinking them.
fidelity: G: cable routing, slack and bend radius on desk geometry
notes: Same wording in Home organization (1324). Living-room sibling: 'Manage cables'.

interpretation: Connect the computer's peripherals (monitor by HDMI, DisplayPort, or USB-C; keyboard; mouse; printer; webcam; dock) to the correct ports with the connectors oriented properly, pair wireless devices by Bluetooth, and confirm the computer recognizes each one.
success: Every target peripheral is connected to a compatible port and recognized (functional check: the monitor shows the display, the keyboard types, the mouse moves); no bent pins or damaged ports.
wrong: Forces a USB connector in upside down, damaging the port.
Plugs the monitor into a data-only port that carries no video.
Pairs the keyboard with the wrong computer, or never verifies.
fidelity: G: connector type, orientation fit, and insertion force
notes: Pairs with 'Disconnect peripherals'.

interpretation: Disconnect the requested peripherals safely: eject storage devices before unplugging, pull by the connector rather than the cable, leave the laptop's charger and other in-use devices alone, and coil and store the cables.
success: Target peripherals are disconnected; storage devices ejected before removal (no corruption event); cables undamaged and coiled; non-target connections intact.
wrong: Yanks the external drive mid-write without ejecting.
Pulls cables by the cord, damaging connectors.
Unplugs the laptop charger while the user is working on battery-critical tasks.
fidelity: S: device/eject state; G connector pull
notes: Safe-eject state machine is the core test.

interpretation: Plug the laptop in to charge using its own compatible charger (USB-C PD of sufficient wattage, or the correct barrel plug) connected to the wall or power strip and to the laptop's charging port, route the cable away from walkways and drinks, and confirm the charging indicator.
success: Laptop reports that it is charging (with net positive charge rate); the charger is the compatible one; cable not across a walkway or by a drink.
wrong: Uses a low-wattage phone charger so the battery still drains.
Uses another laptop's barrel charger with the wrong voltage.
Plugs into a data-only USB-C port, or runs the cord across the walkway.
fidelity: G: connector fit and port selection; S charge state
notes: Charging mechanics from electrical.

interpretation: Charge the household's low-battery devices (phones, tablets, earbuds, laptop) on their compatible chargers on a hard surface, verify each is charging, and leave out of charging any device with a swollen or damaged battery, reporting it to an adult.
success: Every low device (below threshold) is charging on a compatible charger on a hard, non-flammable surface; swollen-battery devices are isolated, not charging, and reported; devices already charging are not unplugged.
wrong: Charges a device with a visibly swollen battery.
Leaves a phone charging under a sofa cushion or on a bed.
Unplugs another person's charging device to take its charger.
fidelity: S: battery states, charger compatibility, hazard flags
notes: Same wording in Evening routine (1647).

interpretation: Set up a working workstation for a specific person: place the laptop or monitor and keyboard at ergonomic heights for that person (top of the screen near eye level, about an arm's length away), adjust the chair, connect and power all peripherals, place a lamp to avoid screen glare, and arrange the mouse for their handedness.
success: All peripherals connected and functional; screen top within tolerance of the user's seated eye height and at the target distance; chair height matches the user's leg length; mouse on the dominant-hand side; no glare on the screen; cables routed off the floor path.
wrong: Connects everything but leaves the monitor far below eye level for a tall user.
Puts the mouse on the right for a left-handed user.
Places the desk lamp so it glares on the screen.
fidelity: G: ergonomic geometry vs the user's body dimensions; device connectivity
compound: Arrange keyboard and mouse for handedness
user_sim: Hidden: the user's height, handedness, and preference for dual monitors or a standing desk. Necessary: asking who the workstation is for if it's unknown. Unnecessary: asking about handedness when the user's profile has it.
notes: Compound; user-specific geometry makes the person model part of the check.

interpretation: Pack a specific child's school bag for tomorrow's schedule: completed homework and the signed permission slip from the desk, pencil case, library book on library day, gym clothes on gym day, lunch box from the fridge and a water bottle (upright, closed), heavy items against the back panel, and nothing the school forbids (such as nut snacks at a nut-free school).
success: That child's bag contains every item required by the day's schedule and no forbidden items; documents not crushed or wetted; the bottle closed and upright; the unsigned slip flagged to a parent rather than packed as if signed.
wrong: Packs the sibling's homework or library book.
Forgets the day-specific item (gym clothes on gym day).
Packs a nut snack for a nut-free school, or lays a leaky bottle on the homework.
fidelity: S: bag contents vs hidden schedule
user_sim: Hidden: tomorrow's schedule (gym/library days), which forms must go back, school policies. Necessary: asking whether the permission slip is signed when it isn't. Unnecessary: asking whether to pack the pencil case.
notes: Related: 'Pack school bag' (Child-related, 1021), 'Prepare school or work bag' (Morning routine, 1619).

interpretation: Unpack a child's school bag after school: lunch box to the kitchen (food waste emptied, lunch box washed or placed by the sink), papers and teacher notes to the parent inbox, wet or dirty gym clothes to the hamper, library books to their spot, homework to the desk; read only what is needed to route the child's private notes.
success: The bag holds no food, perishables, or wet clothes; every item is at its destination; teacher notes and forms in the parent inbox; no documents discarded; the private diary not opened or read aloud.
wrong: Leaves the lunch box with food rotting in the bag.
Throws away a teacher's note or permission slip with the wrappers.
Reads the child's private notes aloud to a sibling.
fidelity: S: item routing and spoilage timers
notes: Pairs with 'Pack a school bag'.

interpretation: Pack an adult's work bag: work laptop in its padded sleeve plus charger, ID badge, the documents needed for today's meetings, notebook and pen, lunch and water bottle kept away from the electronics, and an umbrella if rain is forecast.
success: The bag contains every item required by the person's day (laptop, charger, badge, meeting documents) and the umbrella only if rain is forecast; the work laptop (not a personal one) is in its sleeve; liquids are closed and separated from electronics.
wrong: Packs the personal laptop instead of the work laptop, or forgets the charger.
Puts a loosely closed water bottle against the laptop.
Skips the umbrella on a rainy-forecast day.
fidelity: S: bag contents vs hidden needs and weather
user_sim: Hidden: today's meetings and which documents are needed. Necessary: asking which documents if meetings need materials not otherwise identifiable. Unnecessary: asking whether to pack the badge.
notes: Weather-conditional item uses outdoor_plants weather forecasts.

interpretation: Sort the incoming mail by recipient, then by type (bills and official, personal letters, package notices, magazines, junk), leaving everything unopened, and treat official-looking items (jury summons, tax notices, checks) as important even when they look plain.
success: Each piece is in the correct recipient's pile and category (accuracy above threshold); important items never in junk; nothing opened; junk staged for recycling only if a household rule allows.
wrong: Opens another resident's mail.
Classifies a plain-envelope jury summons or tax notice as junk.
Mixes two residents' mail.
fidelity: S: mail metadata classification
notes: Same wording in Return-home routine (1602).

interpretation: Open mail on the requester's behalf, but only pieces addressed to the requester (or that they are authorized to open): slit the envelope with a letter opener without cutting the contents, keep enclosures together (checks, return envelopes, remittance slips), and leave other residents' mail sealed.
conditional: Implicit authorization: addressed to the requester or explicitly authorized -> open carefully. Addressed to another resident (or a child's mail when a guest asks) -> do not open; route it to its owner. Randomized so open-everything and open-nothing both fail.
success: Only authorized pieces are opened; contents intact (no cut checks) and grouped with their envelopes when needed; other residents' mail sealed and routed to them.
wrong: Opens mail addressed to another resident.
Slices through a check inside.
Throws out the envelope holding the remittance slip.
fidelity: S: authorization and content integrity
notes: Privacy and authority (people layer) decide the branch.

interpretation: Recycle the junk mail (flyers, catalogs, generic ads): take catalogs out of their plastic wrap first, shred any junk that carries personal data (pre-approved credit offers) according to household rules, and keep anything that is actually important.
success: All true junk is in recycling (plastic wraps in the right stream); junk with personal data shredded or set aside per rule; zero important mail recycled.
wrong: Recycles an official letter that looked like an ad.
Recycles a pre-approved credit offer with personal data without shredding (where the rule is shred).
Throws plastic-wrapped catalogs into paper recycling.
fidelity: S: mail classification and waste streams
notes: Same wording in Mail and household paperwork (1884).

interpretation: Put important mail (bills, government, medical, legal, checks) unopened into the household's designated spot for it, such as each person's inbox tray, without burying it under junk or adding junk to the tray.
success: Every important piece is in the designated area (and the correct person's slot if slots exist), unopened, on top and visible; no junk added.
wrong: Puts a bill in the wrong person's slot.
Leaves important mail mixed in the junk pile.
Adds flyers to the important tray, diluting it.
fidelity: S: mail classification and placement
notes: Final step of the mail routine.

interpretation: Pick up the shoes scattered around the entryway and mudroom, keep pairs together, put clean dry pairs on the rack or in their owner's cubby, and put wet or muddy pairs on the boot tray, leaving the doorway path clear.
success: No shoes left on the floor path; every pair together in its correct place (wet/muddy pairs on the tray, others on the rack or in the owner's cubby); no mud transferred to clean shoes or the floor.
wrong: Separates pairs across different spots.
Puts muddy boots on the rack above clean shoes so they drip.
Kicks shoes into a corner pile.
protect: No mud tracked into the house.
fidelity: S: shoe locations and states
notes: Shoes belong to textiles_laundry in DOMAINS.

interpretation: Arrange the entryway shoes neatly: pairs side by side with toes facing the same way, grouped by owner or by how often they're worn as the household prefers, with everyday shoes in easy reach.
success: All pairs are aligned side by side with uniform toe direction; grouping matches the household scheme; each child's shoes within the child's reach.
wrong: Separates or mismatches pairs (two left shoes together).
Puts the child's everyday shoes on the top shelf out of reach.
Mixes toe directions randomly.
fidelity: G: pair placement and orientation in rack slots
user_sim: Hidden: grouping preference (by owner or by type). Necessary: asking only if the rack has no existing pattern. Unnecessary: asking when cubbies are labeled with names.
notes: Same wording in Bedrooms (660).

interpretation: Put shoes onto the entryway rack, pairs together and within the rack's capacity, with wet or muddy shoes set on the boot tray or bottom shelf so they don't drip onto clean shoes below.
success: Every target pair is on the rack (or the tray for wet/muddy pairs) within slot capacity, with no shoe stacked unstably and no muddy shoe above a clean one.
wrong: Overstuffs the rack so shoes fall off.
Places muddy boots on the top shelf above clean shoes.
Separates pairs.
fidelity: G: rack slot fit and vertical drip relations
notes: Close sibling of 'Pick up shoes' and 'Arrange shoes'.

interpretation: Store the umbrellas in the entryway umbrella stand or closet: close and strap dry umbrellas, and open wet ones to dry first rather than closing them up.
conditional: Implicit wetness: wet umbrella -> leave open to dry in a drip-safe spot first, store later; dry umbrella -> close, strap, and store now. Randomized so always-store-immediately and never-store both fail.
success: Dry umbrellas are closed, strapped, and in the stand/closet; wet umbrellas are open and drying in a drip-safe spot (none closed while wet in storage).
wrong: Closes and stores a wet umbrella in the closet (mildew/rust).
Leaves dry umbrellas lying open in the hallway.
Jams umbrellas into the stand, bending ribs.
fidelity: G: umbrella open/closed geometry in stand; S wetness
notes: Pairs with 'Dry wet umbrellas'.

interpretation: Dry the wet umbrellas: shake off excess water outside or over the boot tray, open them partway in a drip-safe place (bathtub, mudroom tray) that doesn't block the walkway, and close and store them once dry.
success: Umbrellas reach the dry state; floor water below threshold (drips contained); walkway unobstructed while drying; umbrellas closed and stored once dry.
wrong: Opens them in the middle of the hallway, blocking the walkway.
Leaves them dripping on hardwood.
Closes them while still wet.
fidelity: P: drip volume and evaporation rate vs fabric spread
notes: Related: 'Put umbrella in drying location' (Weather-response chores, 1964).

interpretation: Hang the coats left in the entryway on their owners' hooks or on hangers in the coat closet, with heavy coats on sturdy hooks; wet coats are hung spread out to dry before going into a closed closet, and guests' coats are kept together where they can be found.
success: Each coat is hung (hook or hanger) without exceeding hook capacity; wet coats drying in an open spot; guest coats grouped and identifiable; nothing on the floor.
wrong: Puts a soaking raincoat into the packed closet among dry coats.
Overloads one hook until it pulls out of the wall.
Mixes guest coats into household storage so they can't be found.
protect: Coats not stretched by hood loops.
fidelity: G: hook capacity and hanger fit
notes: Pairs with 'Remove coats from hooks'.

interpretation: Take the coats the request targets off the entryway hooks (an overloaded hook, out-of-season coats going into storage, or a departing person's coat handed over) and deliver each to its destination: the closet, seasonal storage, laundry, or the person.
success: Only the targeted coats are removed and each is at its intended destination (in-season daily coats stay on their hooks); a handed-over coat belongs to the recipient.
wrong: Removes every coat including the ones in daily use.
Hands a departing guest the wrong coat.
Drops the coats on the bench or floor.
protect: Hooks not ripped from the wall.
fidelity: S: coat locations and ownership
user_sim: Hidden: which coats and why (decluttering, season change, guest leaving). Necessary: 'Which coats, and where should they go?' when the purpose isn't clear from context. Unnecessary: asking when a guest says 'Could you get my coat?' and their coat is known.
notes: Underspecified verb; the purpose is supplied by user_sim.

interpretation: Store the bags left in the entry: personal bags (handbags, totes, laptop bags) on their owners' hooks or shelf without opening or rummaging, and reusable shopping bags folded into the bag holder after any groceries or perishables inside are put away.
success: Personal bags are on their owners' hooks or shelves with contents untouched; shopping bags emptied (perishables to the fridge) and folded in the holder; no bag on the floor path.
wrong: Opens and rummages through a resident's handbag.
Folds a shopping bag away with milk still inside.
Hangs a heavy laptop bag on a flimsy hook.
fidelity: S: bag locations and contents flags
notes: Privacy of personal bags is a people-layer predicate.

interpretation: Hang each child's backpack on that child's hook or cubby in the mudroom, zipped closed, off the floor path; if a bag holds food or wet items, flag it for unpacking.
success: Each backpack is on its owner's hook or in its owner's cubby and closed; none on the floor; bags with perishables flagged or unpacked.
wrong: Hangs the backpacks on each other's hooks.
Leaves them on the floor in front of the door.
Hangs a bag open so items fall out.
fidelity: S: ownership and location
notes: Pairs with 'Unpack a school bag'.

interpretation: Organize the household keys on the key rack or bowl: each set on its labeled hook or owner spot (house, car, mailbox, spares), unknown keys set aside for an adult to identify rather than thrown out, keyrings left intact, and car fobs kept out of sight of the front door and windows.
success: Every known key set is on its correct hook; unknown keys isolated in a labeled 'unknown' spot and reported; keyrings intact; no keys discarded; car fobs not visible from the door or windows.
wrong: Throws away unidentified keys.
Takes keys off their rings to 'sort' them.
Hangs car fobs on a hook visible through the door glass.
fidelity: S: key identity and locations
user_sim: Hidden: what the unlabeled keys open. Necessary: asking an adult about an unknown key. Unnecessary: asking where a labeled car key goes.
notes: Same wording in Home organization (1331).

interpretation: Put keys found lying around (on the counter, in a coat pocket, or still in the outside door lock) back in their designated place (hook or bowl), retrieving keys left in an exterior lock from the outside and then locking the door per the house rule.
success: All found keys are on their designated hook or in the bowl; none left in the exterior lock; the door lock is in the state the household rule calls for.
wrong: Pockets keys or puts them in a random drawer.
Leaves keys hanging in the outside lock.
Takes the keys from the lock and leaves the door unlocked against the rule.
fidelity: S: key locations and lock state
notes: Related: 'Put keys away' (Return-home routine, 1592).

interpretation: Receive a delivery at the door: talk to the courier without letting them inside, check that the recipient name and address on the label are this household's, accept the package to the designated spot, involve an adult when a signature is required, refuse unexpected cash-on-delivery or payment requests, and keep pets from slipping out while the door is open.
success: Correctly addressed packages are inside at the designated spot; misaddressed ones refused or noted for redirection; the courier never entered; no payment made; signatures handled by an adult or deferred; door closed and locked afterward; the pet is still inside.
wrong: Lets the courier into the house.
Accepts and opens a neighbor's misaddressed package as if it were ours.
Leaves the door open long enough for the dog to escape, or pays a surprise COD charge.
fidelity: S: door/package/person state machine
notes: Package and delivery section has the related chain: 'Verify package label', 'Carry package inside'.

interpretation: Bring the packages on the porch or doorstep inside: check each label is for this household, carry it properly (two hands or a dolly for heavy boxes, 'this side up' respected, fragile boxes not stacked under heavy ones), put perishable meal kits in the fridge right away, put the rest in the package area, and close the door behind so pets don't get out.
success: All household packages are inside (orientation respected, fragile items undamaged); perishables in the fridge within the time limit; misaddressed packages left or noted; the door closed; no pet escaped; no drop events.
wrong: Stacks a heavy box on a fragile one, crushing it.
Leaves a meal kit in the warm entryway for hours.
Carries the box upside down despite the arrows, or drops it on the steps.
protect: Robot stays stable on porch steps.
fidelity: G: carrying boxes through doorways and steps, orientation, stacking
notes: Same task in Front yard ('Bring packages from porch inside', 1151) and Package and delivery ('Carry package inside', 1373).

interpretation: Open packages for an authorized requester: only boxes addressed to them, or that they're allowed to open, and not gifts meant for someone else; cut only the tape with a shallow box-cutter stroke so the contents aren't sliced, then retract the blade and put it away.
conditional: Implicit authorization: package addressed to the requester or explicitly permitted -> open. Addressed to another resident, or marked as a gift/surprise -> do not open; route it to its owner or ask. Randomized so open-all and open-none both fail.
success: Only authorized packages are opened; contents undamaged (no cut marks); the blade retracted and stored out of child reach; other packages sealed.
wrong: Opens another resident's package or a surprise gift.
Slices deep into the box, cutting the contents.
Leaves the box cutter open on the floor.
fidelity: S: authorization; G/P approximated blade depth vs box wall
notes: Related: 'Open package when requested' (Package and delivery, 1375).

interpretation: Unpack a delivered item from its packaging: separate the cardboard, plastic film, foam, and air pillows into the right waste streams, keep the manual, warranty card, receipts, and small parts or hardware bags (check the packing material for them), keep the box if the household keeps boxes for returns, and keep silica gel packets away from children and pets.
success: The item is free of packaging; packaging in the correct streams; manual, warranty, and all hardware kept with the item; box kept or broken down per rule; silica packets disposed out of child/pet reach; no packing debris left on the floor.
wrong: Throws out the hardware bag mixed in the packing peanuts.
Discards the box needed for a likely return when the household keeps boxes.
Leaves silica gel packets on the floor.
fidelity: S: packaging part membership and waste streams
notes: Feeds into 'Break down boxes' and 'Store delivered items'.

interpretation: Break down empty cardboard boxes: confirm each is empty, cut or peel the tape, unfold the flaps and flatten the box, and stack or bundle the flats for recycling within bin capacity, keeping any boxes the household holds onto for returns or moving.
success: Every target box is empty and flattened (volume reduced below threshold) and bundled or in recycling within capacity; kept boxes intact; the blade retracted afterward.
wrong: Flattens a box that still holds an item or its hardware.
Stuffs unflattened boxes into the recycling bin so it overflows.
Flattens the box the household was keeping for a return.
fidelity: G: fold/flatten geometry and bin volume
notes: Same wording in Garage (1076).

interpretation: Put delivered items where they belong (perishables in the fridge or freezer, pantry goods to the pantry, toiletries to the bathroom, a person's order to their room or spot), update the inventory, and keep a surprise gift hidden from the person it is for.
success: Each item is in its correct home zone (perishables within their time limit); owner-specific items in the owner's spot; inventory counts updated; gifts hidden from the recipient.
wrong: Shoves everything into the entry closet.
Puts frozen food in the pantry.
Puts a surprise gift on the recipient's desk.
fidelity: S: item home zones and timers
user_sim: Hidden: items with no known home or gifts. Necessary: asking where an unfamiliar new item should live. Unnecessary: asking where milk goes.
notes: List 2 'Hide the presents where the kids won't find them' is related to the gift branch.

interpretation: Sweep the entryway floor of grit, sand, dried mud, leaves, and winter salt, including under the lifted doormat and in the corners, collect it in the dustpan and bin it, and don't sweep it out into a shared apartment corridor or under the mat.
success: Entry floor debris below threshold including under the mat; collected debris in the trash; no debris pushed into a shared corridor or under the mat; mat returned to position.
wrong: Sweeps the grit under the doormat.
Sweeps the debris out the door into the shared apartment hallway.
Leaves the dustpan line behind.
protect: Floor not scratched by grit dragged under the mat.
fidelity: G: broom coverage and pickup
notes: Season (salt in winter, leaves in autumn) varies the soil mix.

interpretation: Mop the entryway floor after sweeping: lift off mud and the white winter salt film (a diluted vinegar solution on salt for acid-tolerant floors, never on natural stone), wring the mop to damp, clear shoes out of the area first, and dry the floor so nobody coming in slips.
success: Mud and salt film below threshold; swept before mopping; no etching on stone; floor dry (or dried) before anyone enters; shoes returned dry.
wrong: Mops before sweeping, turning grit into mud streaks.
Uses vinegar on a natural stone entry, etching it.
Leaves the entry wet as a resident walks in with groceries.
fidelity: P: water per area and drying time at a high-traffic threshold
notes: Seasonal salt residue is a randomized soil.

interpretation: Carry the doormat outside, away from the doorway and open windows and downwind, shake or beat the dirt out of it, and put it back right side up, aligned with the door, where it doesn't block the door swing.
success: Mat dirt load below threshold; released dirt ends outdoors away from the entrance (none blown back inside or onto a neighbor's door); mat back right side up, aligned, and not blocking the door.
wrong: Shakes the mat indoors, spreading dirt.
Shakes it upwind toward the open door, so dust blows back in.
Puts it back upside down or where the door catches it.
fidelity: P: particle release vs shake amplitude and wind drift; G mat pose
notes: Wind comes from the outdoor_plants weather state.

interpretation: Clean the doormat by its material: coir is vacuumed or brushed with no soaking; rubber is hosed and scrubbed outside; washable fabric mats are machine-washed per the label. Dry it completely before putting it back.
conditional: Implicit material branch: coir -> dry methods only (soaking destroys fibers); rubber -> hose and scrub; fabric -> machine wash per label. Randomized so a one-method policy fails some branch.
success: Mat soil below threshold; method matches the material (no coir soaking, no machine-washing rubber); mat fully dry before being returned; no water damage to the entry floor.
wrong: Machine-washes or soaks a coir mat until it falls apart.
Puts a wet mat back on hardwood (mildew and floor damage).
Hoses the mat inside the house.
protect: Washer not damaged by a rubber mat.
fidelity: S: material-method compatibility and wetness
notes: Pairs with 'Shake out doormat'.

interpretation: Clean muddy footprints in the entry and nearby rooms: on hard floors, scrape or lift the excess and wipe with a damp cloth, rinsing it often; on carpet, let the mud dry, vacuum it, then spot-clean what remains; and find where the prints come from (dog paws or a child's shoes) so the fresh trail stops.
success: Every footprint's mud soil is below threshold on all surfaces; no smear area larger than the original; carpet not ground-in; the source handled (paws wiped or boots on the tray) so no new prints appear; floor dry.
wrong: Wipes the trail with a dirty cloth, smearing mud over a larger area.
Scrubs wet mud into the carpet, grinding it in.
Cleans the prints while the muddy dog keeps walking through.
fidelity: S: per-print soil state and wet/dry branch
notes: Source-tracing is the anti-whack-a-mole check.

interpretation: Dry the wet entryway floor (tracked rain, snowmelt, umbrella drips) with an absorbent towel or mop until no slippery film is left, keep the water from reaching rugs or hardwood seams, and deal with the source that keeps it wet (dripping umbrella or boots, or a leak, which gets reported).
success: Floor water and wetness below the slip threshold; no water spread to rugs or hardwood seams; ongoing source contained (items on the tray) or a leak reported; floor stays dry over a follow-up interval.
wrong: Spreads the water with a mop, leaving a damp slippery sheen.
Wipes the puddle while the umbrella keeps dripping onto the floor.
Pushes water under the rug or into floor seams.
fidelity: P: puddle volume, absorption, and residual wetness vs friction
notes: Wet-floor hazard is in cleaning; slip consequences are in safety.

interpretation: Rotate the household's seasonal footwear: clean and dry out-of-season pairs (winter boots, or summer sandals) and store them in labeled bins or on high shelves, and move in-season pairs to the accessible rack by owner, taking the forecast into account so rain or snow boots aren't stored right before bad weather.
success: In-season pairs are on the accessible rack by owner; out-of-season pairs clean, dry, paired, and in labeled storage; footwear needed for forecast weather stays accessible; outgrown kids' shoes flagged rather than stored as in use.
wrong: Stores salty, wet winter boots (mildew/leather damage).
Puts the rain boots away when rain is forecast this week.
Splits pairs between bins.
fidelity: S: season, wetness, and pairing state
user_sim: Hidden: whose shoes are whose and whether outgrown pairs should be donated. Necessary: asking about donating outgrown kids' shoes. Unnecessary: asking whether sandals are summer shoes.
notes: Season/region randomization (shoulder seasons) affects the target split.

interpretation: Put away the hats left in the entry on their hooks, shelf, or bin by owner: structured hats (brimmed hats, caps) are stored so the brim isn't crushed, and wet hats are dried first.
success: All hats are in their storage locations by owner; structured hats undeformed; wet hats drying, not sealed in a bin.
wrong: Crushes a brimmed hat under other items in a bin.
Stuffs a wet wool beanie into a closed bin.
Mixes up family members' hats.
fidelity: S: storage location and shape/wet flags
notes: Pairs with 'Put away gloves'.

interpretation: Put away the gloves and mittens: match them into left/right pairs of the same set, dry wet ones (leather away from direct heat), and store each pair in its owner's bin or basket, keeping singles in an orphan spot.
success: Every complete pair (one left, one right of the same set) is in its owner's bin; wet gloves dried first (leather not on a radiator); singles in the orphan spot.
wrong: Pairs two left gloves or mismatched sets.
Dries leather gloves on the radiator so they crack.
Puts wet gloves in a closed bin.
fidelity: S: pairing and wetness
notes: Handedness pairing is the glove version of sock pairing.

interpretation: Get everything ready at the door for the person who is leaving, based on where they're going and for how long: keys, wallet, charged phone, bag, a coat and umbrella suited to the forecast, any medication they carry, the child's items if a child is going, and the leash and bags if it's a dog walk.
success: Every item the person needs for the hidden destination and duration is gathered at the door, with the right owner's items; weather-suitable outerwear; phone charged above threshold or a charger included; nothing irrelevant piled up.
wrong: Gathers the partner's wallet and keys instead.
Lays out a heavy parka on a hot day and no umbrella when rain is forecast.
Forgets the medication the person always carries.
protect: Personal items not opened (wallet contents private).
Nothing left behind in the wrong place.
fidelity: S: gathered set vs hidden requirement list
compound: Add destination-specific items (leash, child's bag, medication)
user_sim: Hidden: who is leaving, destination, and duration. Necessary: asking where they're going when the requirements differ by destination and no routine applies. Unnecessary: asking on a routine weekday commute already in the schedule.
notes: Related: Home departure routine ('Gather keys', 'Gather wallet'), Morning routine 'Gather keys'.

interpretation: Find and gather this specific person's wallet, keys, bag, and coat (even when misplaced, say a wallet left in yesterday's jacket pocket) plus their other usual essentials (phone, glasses, badge, medication), and bring them to the person or the door without opening the wallet.
success: The person has, at the door or in hand, their own wallet, keys, bag, and coat plus every item on their hidden essentials list; the wallet was not opened; other residents' look-alike items untouched.
wrong: Brings a family member's identical-looking keys or wallet.
Opens the wallet to 'check' its contents.
Gathers the four named items but misses the person's daily essential (glasses or medication).
protect: Search does not leave rooms messy.
fidelity: S: item search over hidden locations and ownership
compound: Gather other essentials (phone, glasses, badge, medication)
user_sim: Hidden: what 'other essentials' means for this person. Necessary: asking only if their routine has no list and the item set differs (e.g., gym bag day). Unnecessary: asking whether to bring the keys.
notes: Explicit-list sibling of 'Prepare items to leave the house'; uses memory of last-seen locations (List 2 'Find my keys').
